question.text: How does North Carolina law treat bicycles, and which laws must bicyclists obey?

answer.text: North Carolina law treats bicycles as vehicles, so bicyclists must obey the same traffic laws as drivers, including the DWI laws.

teaching.text: Bicycles are vehicles in North Carolina, so bicyclists obey the same traffic laws, including DWI laws. Remember: bikes are vehicles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: North Carolina law treats bicycles as vehicles, so bicyclists must obey the same traffic laws as drivers, including the DWI laws.

question.text: Where should drivers expect bicyclists, and when may a bicyclist use the full lane?

answer.text: Drivers should expect bicyclists in the roadway, and traffic conditions may require a bicyclist to use the full travel lane.

teaching.text: Expect bicyclists in the roadway; traffic conditions may require them to use the full lane. Remember: expect bikes in the lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Drivers should expect bicyclists in the roadway, and traffic conditions may require a bicyclist to use the full travel lane.

question.text: Where may bicyclists ride, and what guides their choice?

answer.text: Bicyclists may ride in a bike lane, on a paved shoulder or in a regular travel lane, choosing based on road conditions, hazards and conflicts with right-turning cars.

teaching.text: Bicyclists may use a bike lane, paved shoulder or travel lane, based on conditions and hazards. Remember: lane, shoulder or bike lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists may ride in a bike lane, on a paved shoulder or in a regular travel lane, choosing based on road conditions, hazards and conflicts with right-turning cars.

question.text: Which driver duties also apply to bicyclists?

answer.text: Like drivers, bicyclists must ride on the right side of the road, stop for stop signs and red lights, and give hand signals.

teaching.text: Bicyclists ride on the right, stop for signs and red lights, and give hand signals. Remember: right side, stops, signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Like drivers, bicyclists must ride on the right side of the road, stop for stop signs and red lights, and give hand signals.

question.text: How should you pass a bicyclist, and what is the safest way?

answer.text: Pass a bicyclist only with plenty of clearance and no oncoming traffic in the other lane; changing lanes is the safest way to pass.

teaching.text: Pass a bicyclist with plenty of clearance and no oncoming traffic; changing lanes is safest. Remember: change lanes to pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pass a bicyclist only with plenty of clearance and no oncoming traffic in the other lane; changing lanes is the safest way to pass.

question.text: Which laws govern passing a bicyclist?

answer.text: Passing a bicyclist lawfully means following the same vehicle passing laws that apply to passing any other vehicle.

teaching.text: Passing a bicyclist follows the same passing laws as passing any other vehicle. Remember: same passing laws.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing a bicyclist lawfully means following the same vehicle passing laws that apply to passing any other vehicle.

question.text: Which way should bicyclists ride relative to traffic, and why?

answer.text: Bicyclists should ride with the flow of traffic, never facing it, because drivers often fail to look toward a wrong-way rider.

teaching.text: Bicyclists ride with the flow of traffic, never facing it. Remember: ride with the flow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists should ride with the flow of traffic, never facing it, because drivers often fail to look toward a wrong-way rider.

question.text: Where should you expect bicycles, and which collisions should you watch for?

answer.text: Expect bicycles on every road except where they are expressly banned, and watch for left-cross, drive-out and right-hook collisions.

teaching.text: Expect bicycles on every road unless expressly banned, and watch for left-cross, drive-out and right-hook crashes. Remember: left-cross, drive-out, right-hook.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Expect bicycles on every road except where they are expressly banned, and watch for left-cross, drive-out and right-hook collisions.

question.text: What lights must a bicycle have at night, and how far must they be visible?

answer.text: At night a bicycle must have a front light visible from at least three hundred feet and a rear red light or reflector visible from at least two hundred feet.

teaching.text: At night a bicycle needs a front light seen from three hundred feet and a rear red light or reflector seen from two hundred. Remember: front light, rear red.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night a bicycle must have a front light visible from at least three hundred feet and a rear red light or reflector visible from at least two hundred feet.

question.text: How do the front and rear bicycle light distances differ?

answer.text: A bicycle at night needs a front light seen from three hundred feet but a rear red light or reflector seen from only two hundred feet.

teaching.text: The front light distance is three hundred feet, while the rear is two hundred. Remember: front farther than rear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A bicycle at night needs a front light seen from three hundred feet but a rear red light or reflector seen from only two hundred feet.

question.text: Who must wear an approved bicycle helmet?

answer.text: Every bicycle rider and passenger under age sixteen must wear an approved bicycle helmet and sit on a saddle seat.

teaching.text: Bicycle riders and passengers under sixteen must wear an approved helmet. Remember: young riders wear helmets.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Every bicycle rider and passenger under age sixteen must wear an approved bicycle helmet and sit on a saddle seat.

question.text: Which bicycle passengers must ride in a restraining seat?

answer.text: A bicycle passenger under forty pounds or under forty inches tall must ride in a bicycle restraining seat.

teaching.text: A bicycle passenger under forty pounds or forty inches rides in a restraining seat. Remember: small passengers, restraining seat.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A bicycle passenger under forty pounds or under forty inches tall must ride in a bicycle restraining seat.

question.text: How does the helmet rule's limit differ from the restraining seat rule's limit?

answer.text: The bicycle helmet rule covers riders and passengers under sixteen, while the restraining seat rule covers passengers under forty pounds or forty inches.

teaching.text: The helmet rule goes by age under sixteen, while the seat rule goes by size under forty pounds or forty inches. Remember: helmet by age, seat by size.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The bicycle helmet rule covers riders and passengers under sixteen, while the restraining seat rule covers passengers under forty pounds or forty inches.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: helmet by age, seat by size

question.text: How does the pedestrian share of crash deaths differ between cities and rural areas?

answer.text: In cities about two of every five people killed in motor vehicle crashes are pedestrians, compared with about one in ten in rural areas.

teaching.text: In cities about two of every five crash deaths are pedestrians, compared with one in ten in rural areas. Remember: cities: two in five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In cities about two of every five people killed in motor vehicle crashes are pedestrians, compared with about one in ten in rural areas.

question.text: Where do pedestrians make up the larger share of crash deaths?

answer.text: Pedestrians make up about two of every five crash deaths in cities but only about one in ten in rural areas.

teaching.text: The pedestrian share of crash deaths is larger in cities than in rural areas. Remember: city share is larger.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pedestrians make up about two of every five crash deaths in cities but only about one in ten in rural areas.

question.text: Who are most of the pedestrians killed?

answer.text: Most pedestrians killed are children, elderly people or people who had been drinking.

teaching.text: Most pedestrians killed are children, elderly people or people who had been drinking. Remember: children, elderly, drinkers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most pedestrians killed are children, elderly people or people who had been drinking.

question.text: Which side of the road should pedestrians walk on, and what should they wear?

answer.text: Pedestrians should walk on the left side of the road facing traffic and wear or carry something white.

teaching.text: Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic and wear or carry something white. Remember: walk left, facing traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pedestrians should walk on the left side of the road facing traffic and wear or carry something white.

question.text: What should you carry and be ready to do when walking at night?

answer.text: On foot at night, carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside, since drivers may not see you.

teaching.text: On foot at night, carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside. Remember: flashlight, step aside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On foot at night, carry a flashlight and be ready to step aside, since drivers may not see you.

question.text: How does the pedestrian walking direction differ from the bicyclist riding direction?

answer.text: Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic, which is the opposite of the ride-with-traffic rule for bicyclists.

teaching.text: Pedestrians walk facing traffic, the opposite of bicyclists, who ride with it. Remember: walk against, ride with.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pedestrians walk on the left facing traffic, which is the opposite of the ride-with-traffic rule for bicyclists.

question.text: How do heavy trucks gain speed, and how can their size mislead you?

answer.text: Heavy trucks gain speed slowly, especially uphill, and their size can make them seem slower than they really are.

teaching.text: Heavy trucks gain speed slowly, and their size can make them seem slower than they are. Remember: slow to speed up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Heavy trucks gain speed slowly, especially uphill, and their size can make them seem slower than they really are.

question.text: Why does a truck need extra room to turn, and what should you check before passing?

answer.text: A truck's rear wheels do not follow its front wheels, so it needs extra room to turn; check its turn signal before passing a truck that seems to start a left turn.

teaching.text: A truck's rear wheels do not follow its front wheels, so check its signal before passing a turning truck. Remember: rear wheels do not follow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A truck's rear wheels do not follow its front wheels, so it needs extra room to turn; check its turn signal before passing a truck that seems to start a left turn.

question.text: What happens to truck brakes on downhill runs?

answer.text: Truck brakes heat up on downhill runs, which means the truck needs more distance to stop.

teaching.text: Truck brakes heat up downhill, so the truck needs more distance to stop. Remember: hot brakes, longer stops.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Truck brakes heat up on downhill runs, which means the truck needs more distance to stop.

question.text: How can a large truck beside you affect your steering?

answer.text: Wind currents from a large truck beside you can affect your steering, so give trucks plenty of room.

teaching.text: Wind from a large truck beside you can affect your steering. Remember: truck wind pushes you.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wind currents from a large truck beside you can affect your steering, so give trucks plenty of room.

question.text: What false assumption do drivers make about how high truck drivers sit?

answer.text: Truck drivers sit about twice as high as car drivers, but it is a false assumption that they can see everything around them.

teaching.text: Truck drivers sit high, but they cannot see everything around them. Remember: high seat, still blind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Truck drivers sit about twice as high as car drivers, but it is a false assumption that they can see everything around them.

question.text: Where are a tractor-trailer's no-zones?

answer.text: A tractor-trailer's no-zones reach up to twenty feet in front of the cab, along both sides especially beside the cab, and up to two hundred feet behind.

teaching.text: Truck no-zones reach up to twenty feet in front, along both sides, and up to two hundred feet behind. Remember: front, sides, long rear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A tractor-trailer's no-zones reach up to twenty feet in front of the cab, along both sides especially beside the cab, and up to two hundred feet behind.

question.text: How does the front no-zone compare with the rear no-zone?

answer.text: A truck's front no-zone extends up to twenty feet, but its rear no-zone extends up to two hundred feet.

teaching.text: The front no-zone reaches twenty feet, while the rear no-zone reaches two hundred. Remember: rear zone is longer.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A truck's front no-zone extends up to twenty feet, but its rear no-zone extends up to two hundred feet.

question.text: Why should you not linger in a truck's no-zone, and what is the mirror test?

answer.text: Lingering in a truck's no-zone makes it harder for the trucker to steer clear of danger; if you cannot see the driver in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you.

teaching.text: If you cannot see the truck driver in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you. Remember: no driver in mirror, unseen.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Lingering in a truck's no-zone makes it harder for the trucker to steer clear of danger; if you cannot see the driver in the side mirror, the driver cannot see you.

question.text: How do recreational vehicles differ from cars in size and handling?

answer.text: Recreational vehicles are typically longer, higher and wider than cars, speed up and stop more slowly, and need more turning room.

teaching.text: Recreational vehicles are larger than cars, speed up and stop more slowly, and need more turning room. Remember: longer, slower, wider turns.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Recreational vehicles are typically longer, higher and wider than cars, speed up and stop more slowly, and need more turning room.

question.text: How does following close behind a recreational vehicle affect your view?

answer.text: The closer you get to a recreational vehicle, the more it blocks your view, and its driver has much larger blind spots than a car driver.

teaching.text: The closer you get to a recreational vehicle, the more it blocks your view. Remember: closer means less view.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The closer you get to a recreational vehicle, the more it blocks your view, and its driver has much larger blind spots than a car driver.

question.text: What should you watch for near a vehicle towing a trailer?

answer.text: Near a vehicle towing a trailer, watch for sway in crosswinds or on slippery curves, and know that sudden braking can make the trailer jackknife.

teaching.text: Watch for trailer sway, and know that sudden braking can make a trailer jackknife. Remember: sway and jackknife.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Near a vehicle towing a trailer, watch for sway in crosswinds or on slippery curves, and know that sudden braking can make the trailer jackknife.

question.text: How much clear road may passing a trailer and its towing vehicle take?

answer.text: Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle safely can take a half mile of clear road.

teaching.text: Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle can take a half mile of clear road. Remember: half mile to pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing a trailer and its towing vehicle safely can take a half mile of clear road.

question.text: What two facts should you remember about passing and braking near a trailer?

answer.text: Passing a vehicle towing a trailer may need a half mile of clear road, and braking hard near it risks a jackknife.

teaching.text: Passing a trailer may need a half mile, and hard braking near it risks a jackknife. Remember: long pass, gentle brakes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing a vehicle towing a trailer may need a half mile of clear road, and braking hard near it risks a jackknife.

question.text: What right-of-way consideration do motorcycle and moped riders get?

answer.text: Give motorcycle and moped riders the same right-of-way consideration as any other driver.

teaching.text: Give motorcycle and moped riders the same right-of-way consideration as any driver. Remember: riders get equal rights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Give motorcycle and moped riders the same right-of-way consideration as any other driver.

question.text: How do you pass a motorcycle?

answer.text: A motorcycle is entitled to its full lane, so pass it by changing lanes exactly as you would for a larger vehicle.

teaching.text: A motorcycle owns its full lane, so pass it by changing lanes. Remember: full lane, change lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A motorcycle is entitled to its full lane, so pass it by changing lanes exactly as you would for a larger vehicle.

question.text: Where do mopeds ride in the lane, and how much room must you leave when passing?

answer.text: Mopeds ride on the right side of the lane, and when passing one you must stay at least two feet to its left.

teaching.text: Mopeds ride on the right of the lane; pass at least two feet to the left. Remember: moped right, leave room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Mopeds ride on the right side of the lane, and when passing one you must stay at least two feet to its left.

question.text: How does passing a motorcycle differ from passing a moped?

answer.text: To pass a motorcycle you change lanes because it owns its full lane, while to pass a moped you keep at least two feet to its left.

teaching.text: Change lanes to pass a motorcycle, but keep at least two feet left of a moped. Remember: motorcycle lane, moped gap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To pass a motorcycle you change lanes because it owns its full lane, while to pass a moped you keep at least two feet to its left.

question.text: Why leave extra room when passing any cyclist?

answer.text: Leave enough room when passing any cyclist so your vehicle's windstream cannot make the rider lose control.

teaching.text: Leave enough room passing any cyclist that your windstream cannot upset the rider. Remember: windstream can upset riders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Leave enough room when passing any cyclist so your vehicle's windstream cannot make the rider lose control.

question.text: When should you look especially for motorcycles and mopeds?

answer.text: Motorcycles and mopeds can be completely hidden in blind spots, so look for them before turning, changing lanes or pulling out, especially when turning left.

teaching.text: Riders can hide in blind spots, so look before turning, changing lanes or pulling out. Remember: look before turning left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcycles and mopeds can be completely hidden in blind spots, so look for them before turning, changing lanes or pulling out, especially when turning left.

question.text: In motorcycle crashes involving a car, who is usually at fault?

answer.text: About two-thirds of North Carolina motorcycle crashes involve a car, and in most of them the car driver is at fault, often saying the motorcycle went unseen.

teaching.text: In most car and motorcycle crashes, the car driver is at fault, often saying the rider went unseen. Remember: car drivers often miss them.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: About two-thirds of North Carolina motorcycle crashes involve a car, and in most of them the car driver is at fault, often saying the motorcycle went unseen.

question.text: How does motorcycle stopping compare with car stopping?

answer.text: Most motorcycles stop faster than cars, but they stop more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces where hard braking could cause a fall.

teaching.text: Motorcycles usually stop faster than cars, but more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces. Remember: usually faster, sometimes slower.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most motorcycles stop faster than cars, but they stop more slowly with a passenger or on poor surfaces where hard braking could cause a fall.

question.text: When do motorcycles stop more slowly than usual?

answer.text: Motorcycles usually stop faster than cars, but more slowly with a passenger or on poor road surfaces.

teaching.text: Solo on a good surface, a motorcycle stops faster; loaded or on a poor surface, it stops more slowly. Remember: passenger or poor surface.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcycles usually stop faster than cars, but more slowly with a passenger or on poor road surfaces.

question.text: Which surface hazards can upset a rider ahead, and what does a wobbling rider suggest?

answer.text: Sand, gravel, wet leaves or water on the pavement can make a rider ahead lose control, and a wobbling or hesitant rider is likely a beginner who needs extra room.

teaching.text: Sand, gravel, wet leaves or water can upset a rider, and a wobbling rider needs extra room. Remember: gravel, leaves, beginners.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Sand, gravel, wet leaves or water on the pavement can make a rider ahead lose control, and a wobbling or hesitant rider is likely a beginner who needs extra room.

question.text: How much room should you give a motorcycle or moped on slippery roads?

answer.text: Never crowd a motorcycle or moped, and leave a longer following distance on slippery roads because two wheels are easily destabilized.

teaching.text: Never crowd a motorcycle or moped, and leave a longer gap on slippery roads. Remember: never crowd two wheels.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never crowd a motorcycle or moped, and leave a longer following distance on slippery roads because two wheels are easily destabilized.

question.text: Where should you give riders extra room?

answer.text: Give riders extra room at railroad crossings, on rough roads and on metal surfaces such as steel bridge joints and grating.

teaching.text: Give riders extra room at railroad crossings, on rough roads and on metal surfaces. Remember: rails, rough roads, metal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Give riders extra room at railroad crossings, on rough roads and on metal surfaces such as steel bridge joints and grating.

question.text: What helmet must moped riders and passengers wear?

answer.text: Moped riders and all passengers must wear a helmet meeting Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard two hundred eighteen with the retention strap fastened.

teaching.text: Moped riders and all passengers must wear an approved helmet with the strap fastened. Remember: approved helmet, strap fastened.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Moped riders and all passengers must wear a helmet meeting Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard two hundred eighteen with the retention strap fastened.

question.text: How does North Carolina define a moped?

answer.text: North Carolina defines a moped as a two- or three-wheeled vehicle with a motor of no more than fifty cubic centimeters and no external shifting device.

teaching.text: A moped has two or three wheels, a motor of no more than fifty cubic centimeters and no external shifter. Remember: small motor, no shifter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: North Carolina defines a moped as a two- or three-wheeled vehicle with a motor of no more than fifty cubic centimeters and no external shifting device.

question.text: What is a moped's top speed limit, and what about faster models?

answer.text: A moped's top speed may not exceed thirty miles per hour, and mopeds built to go faster are illegal to use in North Carolina.

teaching.text: A moped's top speed may not exceed thirty miles per hour. Remember: faster models are illegal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A moped's top speed may not exceed thirty miles per hour, and mopeds built to go faster are illegal to use in North Carolina.

question.text: What does a moped operator need to ride on a public road?

answer.text: To operate a moped on a public road you must be at least sixteen and hold a valid N.C. driver license or ID card, and impaired driving laws apply to moped riders too.

teaching.text: A moped operator must be at least sixteen with a valid N.C. license or ID card. Remember: license or ID required.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To operate a moped on a public road you must be at least sixteen and hold a valid N.C. driver license or ID card, and impaired driving laws apply to moped riders too.

question.text: What are the three moped limits for motor, speed and operator age?

answer.text: A moped is limited to a motor of fifty cubic centimeters and a top speed of thirty miles per hour, and its operator must be at least sixteen.

teaching.text: Moped limits are a fifty cubic centimeter motor, thirty miles per hour, and an operator at least sixteen. Remember: motor, speed, age limits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A moped is limited to a motor of fifty cubic centimeters and a top speed of thirty miles per hour, and its operator must be at least sixteen.

question.text: How should moped riders position themselves in traffic?

answer.text: Moped riders should keep right in the lane, never share a lane with another vehicle, and never squeeze between parked cars and moving traffic at an intersection.

teaching.text: Moped riders keep right, never share a lane, and never squeeze between parked cars and traffic. Remember: keep right, never share.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Moped riders should keep right in the lane, never share a lane with another vehicle, and never squeeze between parked cars and moving traffic at an intersection.

question.text: What should moped riders wear and use to be seen?

answer.text: Moped riders should wear light or bright clothing and use electric turn signals if fitted, or hand signals otherwise.

teaching.text: Moped riders wear bright clothing and use turn signals or hand signals. Remember: bright clothes, signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Moped riders should wear light or bright clothing and use electric turn signals if fitted, or hand signals otherwise.

question.text: What must every moped have since registration became required?

answer.text: Since July two thousand fifteen, every moped must be registered with the DMV and display a license plate on the rear at all times.

teaching.text: Every moped must be registered with the DMV and show a rear license plate at all times. Remember: registered, rear plate.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Since July two thousand fifteen, every moped must be registered with the DMV and display a license plate on the rear at all times.

question.text: What can a moped owner use as proof of ownership without the certificate of origin?

answer.text: A moped owner without the manufacturer's certificate of origin can use form MVR-fifty-eight, an affidavit of facts, as proof of ownership.

teaching.text: Without the certificate of origin, a moped owner can use an affidavit of facts as proof of ownership. Remember: affidavit of facts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A moped owner without the manufacturer's certificate of origin can use form MVR-fifty-eight, an affidavit of facts, as proof of ownership.

question.text: What do moped registration and the ownership affidavit have in common?

answer.text: Moped registration has been required since July two thousand fifteen, and an owner lacking the certificate of origin may file form MVR-fifty-eight instead.

teaching.text: Moped registration is required, and an affidavit can stand in for the certificate of origin. Remember: register, or file affidavit.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Moped registration has been required since July two thousand fifteen, and an owner lacking the certificate of origin may file form MVR-fifty-eight instead.

question.text: Who is held responsible when litter comes from a vehicle?

answer.text: Littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle.

teaching.text: Littering is illegal, and the driver is held responsible for litter thrown or blown from the vehicle. Remember: driver owns the litter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Littering is illegal in North Carolina, and the driver is held responsible when litter is thrown or blown from the vehicle.

question.text: How does the fine for a first littering conviction differ from a repeat?

answer.text: A first littering conviction is fined two hundred fifty dollars to one thousand, dollars while a repeat within three years is fined five hundred dollars to two thousand dollars.

teaching.text: A repeat littering conviction within three years carries a higher fine than a first. Remember: repeat fines run higher.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A first littering conviction is fined two hundred fifty dollars to one thousand, dollars while a repeat within three years is fined five hundred dollars to two thousand dollars.
